questions.answer: Explain failure handling, cancellation, retries and why result order is preserved.

questions.question: What is semantic HTML?
questions.answer: Use elements according to meaning: header, nav, main, article, section, button, form, footer and so on. It improves accessibility, maintainability and browser behavior.

questions.question: div vs section?
questions.answer: div has no semantic meaning; section represents a thematic grouping and normally has an identifiable purpose/heading.

questions.question: article vs section?
questions.answer: article is suitable for self-contained/distributable content; section groups related content.

questions.question: main vs div?
questions.answer: main identifies the primary content of the document and creates a useful accessibility landmark.

questions.question: What is the DOM?
questions.answer: The browser's object representation of the document, which scripts and browser APIs can inspect and manipulate.

questions.question: What is the viewport meta tag?
questions.answer: It controls the mobile layout viewport and scaling. A common responsive setting uses width=device-width.

questions.question: Why is alt text important?
questions.answer: It provides a text alternative for meaningful images. Decorative images can use empty alt text.

questions.question: img vs background-image?
questions.answer: Use img for content images needing semantics/alt text; background-image is generally for decoration.

questions.question: label vs placeholder?
questions.answer: A label identifies a control and should remain available. Placeholder is only a hint.

questions.question: button vs anchor?
questions.answer: button performs an action; anchor navigates. Using the semantic element gives correct keyboard and accessibility behavior.

questions.question: GET vs POST form?
questions.answer: GET suits retrieval/search and URL-addressable queries; POST is generally used for state-changing submissions.

questions.question: What is progressive enhancement?
questions.answer: Build a functional baseline using platform capabilities, then enhance with CSS and JavaScript.

questions.question: What is ARIA?
questions.answer: Accessibility semantics/states used when native HTML cannot express the required behavior. Prefer native semantics first.

questions.question: Why lang attribute?
questions.answer: It identifies document language for assistive technology and text processing.

questions.question: async vs defer?
questions.answer: Both avoid the blocking behavior of classic synchronous scripts. defer preserves order and runs after parsing; async runs when ready and does not guarantee order.

questions.question: Why can script loading affect performance?
questions.answer: Synchronous scripts can block parsing/execution. Deferring non-critical code improves initial loading.

questions.question: What is a form's accessible error strategy?
questions.answer: Associate errors with fields, identify the problem clearly, preserve keyboard access and provide predictable focus behavior.

questions.question: What are landmark elements?
questions.answer: Semantic regions such as header, nav, main, aside and footer help assistive technology navigate page structure.

questions.question: Why should heading levels be meaningful?
questions.answer: Headings communicate document structure. Do not choose heading levels merely for font size; style them with CSS.
questions.code: Orders

questions.question: Explain the box model.
questions.answer: Content, padding, border and margin. box-sizing controls whether declared dimensions include padding/border; border-box is often easier to reason about.

questions.question: What is margin collapse?
questions.answer: Certain vertical margins in normal flow can collapse into one margin, which can produce surprising spacing.

questions.question: Explain specificity.
questions.answer: Specificity ranks competing selectors after cascade origin/layer considerations. IDs outrank classes/attributes/pseudo-classes, which outrank element selectors.

questions.question: What is the cascade?
questions.answer: The browser resolves competing declarations using origin/importance, cascade layers, specificity and source order.

questions.question: What is inheritance?
questions.answer: Some properties naturally inherit from ancestors, such as color and font properties; others do not.

questions.question: Flexbox?
questions.answer: A one-dimensional layout system for arranging items along a main axis with cross-axis alignment.

questions.question: Grid?
questions.answer: A two-dimensional layout system for rows and columns.

questions.question: Flex vs Grid?
questions.answer: Use Flex for primarily one-dimensional layouts and Grid when rows and columns both matter.

questions.question: justify-content vs align-items?
questions.answer: They control distribution/alignment along different axes depending on the layout.

questions.question: What is flex:1?
questions.answer: Commonly expands to grow/shrink with a zero basis, allowing siblings to share available space.

questions.question: position modes?
questions.answer: relative offsets from normal position; absolute leaves normal flow and uses a containing block; fixed is viewport-oriented; sticky sticks within scroll constraints.

questions.question: What creates a stacking context?
questions.answer: Properties such as positioned z-index elements, opacity, transforms and isolation can create independent stacking contexts.

questions.question: Why does z-index not work?
questions.answer: The element may be trapped in another stacking context. Increasing z-index inside the wrong context cannot cross that context.

questions.question: CSS specificity hell?
questions.answer: Overly specific selectors make overrides difficult. Prefer predictable scoping, low specificity and design tokens.

questions.question: CSS custom properties?
questions.answer: Runtime variables such as --color-primary that participate in the cascade and are excellent for theming.

questions.question: Sass variables vs CSS variables?
questions.answer: Sass variables are compile-time; CSS custom properties exist at runtime and can change through the cascade.

questions.question: Responsive design?
questions.answer: Adapt layout and interaction to viewport/container size using flexible units, media/container queries and responsive assets.

questions.question: Media vs container queries?
questions.answer: Media queries react to viewport/device conditions; container queries react to the size of a component's container.

questions.question: Mobile-first CSS?
questions.answer: Start with the base/small-screen layout and progressively enhance for larger conditions.

questions.question: BEM?
questions.answer: Block Element Modifier naming methodology that makes class relationships explicit.

questions.question: CSS Modules?
questions.answer: Build-time scoping of class names to reduce global collisions.

questions.question: CSS-in-JS pros/cons?
questions.answer: Can colocate styling and dynamic logic, but may add runtime/build complexity and ecosystem trade-offs.

questions.question: Utility-first CSS?
questions.answer: Compose small utility classes for styling. It improves consistency but needs conventions to keep markup readable.

questions.question: SCSS architecture?
questions.answer: Separate tokens, mixins, base styles, component styles and utilities; avoid deep nesting and global coupling.

questions.question: Dark mode?
questions.answer: Use semantic CSS variables driven by a theme class/data attribute or prefers-color-scheme.

questions.question: Avoid CSS leakage?
questions.answer: Use scoped styles, disciplined naming, CSS Modules or cascade layers and minimize global selectors.

questions.question: Reflow vs repaint?
questions.answer: Reflow/layout recalculates geometry; repaint redraws pixels. Some changes trigger both.

questions.question: Why prefer transform/opacity for many animations?
questions.answer: They can avoid repeated layout calculations and can be handled efficiently by the rendering pipeline; always measure.

questions.question: prefers-reduced-motion?
questions.answer: A media feature allowing users to request reduced animation/motion for accessibility.

questions.question: Design tokens?
questions.answer: Named values for color, spacing, typography, radius and other design decisions that keep a design system consistent.

questions.question: SCSS vs CSS Modules vs component library?
questions.answer: They solve different problems. A component library gives reusable UI behavior; CSS Modules scope styles; SCSS provides preprocessing. A large ERP can combine a design system with scoped component styles.

questions.question: What is a design system?
questions.answer: A coordinated set of design tokens, components, patterns, accessibility rules and documentation.

questions.question: How do you prevent a design system becoming a bottleneck?
questions.answer: Define contribution standards, ownership, versioning and extension points. Keep primitives stable and composable.

questions.question: How do you implement theme switching?
questions.answer: Use semantic tokens and a root theme class/data attribute so components consume variables rather than hard-coded colors.

questions.question: How do you handle responsive ERP layouts?
questions.answer: Use flexible grid/flex layouts, breakpoints and container queries where component-level responsiveness helps.

questions.question: How do you review CSS?
questions.answer: Check semantics, scope, specificity, responsive behavior, accessibility, duplication and whether a value belongs in a shared token/component.

questions.question: What is CSS architecture's biggest goal?
questions.answer: Predictability. A developer should know where a style comes from and how safely it can be changed.

questions.question: What is Node.js?
questions.answer: A JavaScript runtime built on V8 with event-driven, non-blocking I/O. It is strong for I/O-heavy APIs but synchronous CPU work can block the event loop.

questions.question: Explain Node's event loop.
questions.answer: Node coordinates asynchronous operations and executes callbacks when work becomes ready. Long synchronous JavaScript prevents other callbacks from progressing.

questions.question: What is libuv?
questions.answer: The cross-platform library behind Node's event loop and several asynchronous I/O/thread-pool facilities.

questions.question: What uses Node's thread pool?
questions.answer: Some filesystem, DNS and CPU-oriented library operations can use the libuv thread pool; exact behavior depends on API/platform.

questions.question: process.nextTick vs Promise microtasks?
questions.answer: Both are high-priority mechanisms, but Node schedules nextTick specially. Excessive nextTick can starve other event-loop work.

questions.question: setImmediate vs setTimeout(0)?
questions.answer: They execute in different scheduling phases and their ordering can depend on context. Avoid claiming one always wins.

questions.question: worker_threads?
questions.answer: Separate JavaScript execution contexts for CPU-heavy work so the main event-loop thread remains responsive.

questions.question: cluster vs worker_threads?
questions.answer: Cluster uses multiple Node processes; worker_threads use additional threads inside a process. They address different scaling/workload problems.

questions.question: What is backpressure?
questions.answer: When a producer is faster than a consumer. Streams provide flow control so memory does not grow uncontrollably.

questions.question: Buffer?
questions.answer: Node's representation of raw binary data used for files, sockets and protocols.

questions.question: Stream?
questions.answer: Incremental data processing through readable, writable, duplex and transform streams.

questions.question: EventEmitter?
questions.answer: A publish/subscribe event mechanism used by many Node APIs.

questions.question: Environment variables?
questions.answer: External configuration accessed through process.env; secrets must be managed securely.

questions.question: Graceful shutdown?
questions.answer: Stop accepting new work, finish/timeout active work, close connections and exit cleanly on signals such as SIGTERM.

questions.question: Node memory leak?
questions.answer: Unintended retained references such as listeners, timers, caches or global objects prevent garbage collection.

questions.question: Node API performance?
questions.answer: Measure first; optimize DB latency, serialization, synchronous work, payload size, caching and connection usage.

questions.question: Horizontal vs vertical scaling?
questions.answer: Vertical adds resources to one machine; horizontal adds instances and requires appropriate stateless/shared infrastructure.

questions.question: Stateless API?
questions.answer: Each request contains enough information to process it without relying on local instance-only session state.

questions.question: How do you avoid blocking Node?
questions.answer:
Avoid synchronous heavy operations, chunk CPU work and move heavy computation to workers/services.
Express builds on the Node HTTP server and adds routing/middleware abstractions.

questions.question: Explain Express request lifecycle.
questions.answer: HTTP request → middleware in registration order → matching route → controller/service work → response; errors flow to error-handling middleware.

questions.question: Why does middleware order matter?
questions.answer: Express executes middleware in order. Authentication registered after a route cannot protect that route.

questions.question: app.use?
questions.answer: Registers middleware, optionally under a path prefix.

questions.question: app.get/app.post?
questions.answer: Registers handlers for GET/POST routes.

questions.question: Router vs app?
questions.answer: Router modularizes related routes and middleware so large applications do not become one file.

questions.question: Express architecture?
questions.answer: A practical structure is routes → controllers → services → repositories/data access, plus cross-cutting middleware.

questions.question: Controller vs service?
questions.answer: Controller owns HTTP concerns; service owns reusable business logic.

questions.question: Repository layer?
questions.answer: Encapsulates persistence/database details and keeps business logic independent of storage.

questions.question: Request validation?
questions.answer: Validate body, params and query against runtime schemas before business logic.

questions.question: Async error handling?
questions.answer: Ensure rejected Promises reach centralized error handling through framework-supported async handling or a consistent async wrapper.

questions.question: 400 vs 422?
questions.answer: 400 commonly means malformed request; 422 is commonly used for semantically invalid input. Consistency is more important than arguing one universal code.

questions.question: Authentication middleware?
questions.answer: Verify credentials/token, establish identity/claims in request context, then continue.

questions.question: Authorization?
questions.answer: Check permissions/resource ownership server-side for every protected operation.

questions.question: Express security?
questions.answer: Validate input, configure CORS deliberately, secure headers, rate-limit sensitive routes, avoid stack-trace leakage and keep dependencies patched.

questions.question: File upload security?
questions.answer: Validate size/type, avoid trusting client filenames/MIME, stream where appropriate and scan/store safely.

questions.question: Structured logging?
questions.answer: Log request ID, method, route, status, duration and safe context; never log secrets.

questions.question: Idempotency?
questions.answer: Repeating the same operation produces the same intended effect. Important for retryable mutations such as payments/orders.

questions.question: API versioning?
questions.answer: Use a deliberate URL/header/content-negotiation strategy and prefer backward-compatible evolution.

questions.question: Offset vs cursor pagination?
questions.answer: Offset is simple; cursor/range pagination is often more stable/scalable for large changing datasets.

questions.question: Rate limiting?
questions.answer: Limit request frequency to protect availability and prevent abuse.

questions.question: What is CORS configuration risk?
questions.answer: Overly broad origins/credentials can expose APIs. Configure allowed origins, methods and credentials deliberately.

questions.question: What is MongoDB?
questions.answer: A document-oriented database using BSON documents in collections.

questions.question: Document vs collection?
questions.answer: A document is an individual BSON record; a collection groups documents.

questions.question: Embed vs reference?
questions.answer: Embed tightly owned, bounded data read together. Reference shared, independently changing or unbounded data.

questions.question: What is an index?
questions.answer: A data structure that speeds queries by avoiding full collection scans, at the cost of storage/write overhead.

questions.question: How choose indexes?
questions.answer: Start from actual query/filter/sort patterns and validate using explain. Avoid indexing every field.

questions.question: Compound index?
questions.answer: An index over multiple fields; field order matters for supported query patterns.

questions.question: What is aggregation?
questions.answer: A pipeline of stages that transforms, filters, groups and summarizes documents.

questions.question: $lookup?
questions.answer: A join-like aggregation stage. Useful when needed, but excessive lookups may indicate a modeling/query issue.

questions.question: Upsert?
questions.answer: Update a matching document or insert one if no match exists.

questions.question: ObjectId?
questions.answer: A common MongoDB identifier containing timestamp-related and uniqueness information.

questions.question: Atomicity?
questions.answer: Single-document writes are atomic. Multi-document transactions can provide transactional guarantees when needed.

questions.question: When use transactions?
questions.answer: When multiple writes must succeed/fail together and data modeling alone cannot provide the needed consistency.

questions.question: Schema validation?
questions.answer: Database-level validation rules that protect the persistence boundary.

questions.question: Mongo injection prevention?
questions.answer: Validate types/allowed fields and construct queries explicitly instead of blindly merging request objects.

questions.question: Projection?
questions.answer: Select only required fields to reduce data transfer and processing.

questions.question: explain()?
questions.answer: Shows query execution details such as indexes and documents examined, helping diagnose slow queries.

questions.question: Slow Mongo query?
questions.answer: Inspect explain, indexes, selectivity, returned fields, pagination and data model; measure before/after.

questions.question: Connection pooling?
questions.answer: Reusable database connections managed by the driver instead of opening a new connection for each request.

questions.question: Mongo pagination?
questions.answer: skip/limit can work for simple cases; indexed cursor/range pagination is often better for large or changing datasets.

questions.question: Audit history?
questions.answer: Store immutable events/history with actor, action, timestamp and resource identifiers.

questions.question: Soft delete?
questions.answer: Store a deletion marker/timestamp and consistently filter it from normal queries; account for indexes/uniqueness.

questions.question: How do you model ERP transactions?
questions.answer:
Keep a transaction document bounded and embed fields that belong to the transaction; reference large/shared master data such as products/customers where independent lifecycle and reuse justify it.
In production, centralize and reuse the client/connection pool rather than connecting for every request. The official MongoDB Node.js driver supports Atlas, Enterprise and Community deployments.

questions.question: Rendering vs commit?
questions.answer: Rendering calculates the next UI; commit applies required host changes. Effects follow React's effect lifecycle.

questions.question: Why must render be pure?
questions.answer: React may render more than once and optimize/restart work. Side effects during render make behavior unpredictable.

questions.question: Strict Mode?
questions.answer: Development checks that expose unsafe patterns; apparent repeated setup/render behavior should not be mistaken for production behavior.

questions.question: State as a snapshot?
questions.answer: Each render sees its own state snapshot. setState schedules another render; it does not mutate the current render's variable.

questions.question: Why does setCount(count+1) twice usually add one?
questions.answer: Both expressions use the same snapshot. Functional updates apply sequential transformations.

questions.question: Automatic batching?
questions.answer: React can group multiple state updates into fewer renders in many contexts, improving efficiency.

questions.question: Stale closure?
questions.answer: A callback retains values from its creation render. Later execution may see old state; use functional updates, dependencies or refs as appropriate.

questions.question: useRef?
questions.answer: Persistent mutable value that does not trigger re-render when changed.

questions.question: When not to use useEffect?
questions.answer: Do not use it for simple derived data, direct event responses or state synchronization that can be expressed during rendering.

questions.question: Why do effects loop?
questions.answer: An effect updates a dependency that triggers it again. Fix the underlying synchronization relationship.

questions.question: Rules of Hooks?
questions.answer: Call hooks only at the top level of React components or custom hooks, not conditionally or inside arbitrary functions.

questions.question: Compound components?
questions.answer: Related components share state/context to create a flexible declarative API, such as Tabs.

questions.question: Render props?
questions.answer: Pass a rendering function to a component. Hooks/composition often provide simpler modern alternatives.

questions.question: HOC?
questions.answer: A function that accepts a component and returns an enhanced component. Useful in some libraries but can add wrapper complexity.

questions.question: State colocation?
questions.answer: Keep state close to the components that actually use it to reduce unnecessary updates and clarify ownership.

questions.question: Lifting state?
questions.answer: Move shared state to the nearest common ancestor when siblings need coordination.

questions.question: Derived state?
questions.answer: A value calculated from props/state. Avoid storing duplicates that can become inconsistent.

questions.question: Context overuse?
questions.answer: Broad, frequently changing context can cause many consumers to re-render; split contexts or use a targeted state mechanism.

questions.question: Large form optimization?
questions.answer: Localize field updates, avoid rerendering the whole form, validate at sensible times and virtualize large dynamic sections if needed.

questions.question: Large table optimization?
questions.answer: Use server filtering/pagination, virtualization, stable row identity and measured memoization.

questions.question: Suspense?
questions.answer: A mechanism for coordinating UI around supported asynchronous rendering boundaries and fallbacks.

questions.question: Error boundaries?
questions.answer: Catch rendering errors in descendant trees and show fallback UI; they do not replace arbitrary async error handling.

questions.question: API error states?
questions.answer: Represent loading/success/error explicitly, cancel stale requests and provide actionable feedback.

questions.question: Prevent stale responses?
questions.answer: Abort previous requests or use request IDs and only commit the latest response.

questions.question: Optimistic UI?
questions.answer: Update immediately assuming success, then confirm or roll back. It improves responsiveness but needs conflict/rollback handling.

questions.question: Idempotent UI actions?
questions.answer: Prevent repeated clicks/retries from creating duplicate mutations; combine UI guards with server idempotency for important operations.

questions.question: Reusable component design?
questions.answer: Small API, composition, internal accessibility and no unnecessary business assumptions.

questions.question: When is a component too large?
questions.answer: When it owns unrelated concerns, mixes API/business/UI complexity and becomes hard to test. Split by responsibility/domain.

questions.question: When should you create a shared component?
questions.answer: When behavior/semantics repeat and requirements are stable. Visual similarity alone is not enough.

questions.question: React Compiler impact?
questions.answer: It can automatically memoize components/hooks at build time, reducing routine manual memoization. It does not solve poor state ownership, huge data processing or network waterfalls. Current React guidance recommends relying on compiler optimization for new code where enabled and using manual memoization when precise control is needed.

questions.question: React Compiler directives?
questions.answer: The compiler supports directives such as use memo and use no memo for fine-grained compilation control in supported modes.

questions.question: useTransition?
questions.answer: Marks selected state updates as non-urgent so urgent interactions remain responsive.

questions.question: useDeferredValue?
questions.answer: Allows a slower part of the UI to lag behind a rapidly changing value.

questions.question: Transition vs deferred value?
questions.answer: Use transition when you control the state update; use deferred value when you already have a value and want a dependent expensive UI to lag.

questions.question: How do you optimize a React page?
questions.answer: Measure with Profiler/browser tools, identify rendering/data/network bottlenecks and fix the largest measured cause first.

questions.question: How do you handle 100K records?
questions.answer: Do not render all at once. Use server-side filtering/pagination, virtualization and efficient state/data structures.

questions.question: What is perceived performance?
questions.answer:
How quickly the user feels the interface responds. Skeletons, optimistic updates, transitions and progressive loading can improve perception while real performance is also addressed.
Functional updates use the latest queued state, so this pattern increments by two.

questions.question: ERP page takes 8 seconds to become usable. What do you investigate?
questions.answer: Measure server response, HTML delivery, JavaScript bundle, route-level code splitting, API waterfalls, large lookup requests, hydration/client work and long main-thread tasks.

questions.question: Search results arrive out of order. Fix?
questions.answer: Debounce input, cancel obsolete requests with AbortController and/or use request IDs so only the latest response updates state.

questions.question: MongoDB query is slow only for large customers. Fix?
questions.answer: Capture the query shape, inspect explain plans, verify indexes/selectivity, review pagination and data modeling and measure again.

questions.question: Express becomes slow during CPU-heavy reporting. Why?
questions.answer: Synchronous CPU work blocks Node's event loop. Move heavy work to worker threads/services or precompute where appropriate.

questions.question: CSS change breaks unrelated pages. Likely cause?
questions.answer: Global selectors, high specificity, shared class names or theme leakage. Use scoped styles/design tokens and reduce coupling.

questions.question: Accessibility audit finds clickable divs. Fix?
questions.answer: Use semantic buttons/links when possible. If a true custom widget is required, implement keyboard behavior, focus and correct semantics.

questions.question: Next.js secret appears in browser bundle. Fix?
questions.answer: Trace imports/props/environment variables and move secret access into server-only code; never expose server secrets through public client configuration.

questions.question: Legacy React app modernization?
questions.answer: Inventory risk, establish tests, upgrade incrementally, improve tooling and architecture domain-by-domain, and measure changes rather than rewriting everything at once.

questions.question: Team wants every API response in Redux. Agree?
questions.answer: No. Separate server state from shared client state and local UI state. Avoid duplicate caches that create invalidation problems.

questions.question: Reusable component has 25 props. What does it suggest?
questions.answer: It may be representing too many variants. Consider composition, slots or splitting responsibilities rather than adding more boolean props.

sections.title: L1. How to Explain the MPO Project in 60–90 Seconds

questions.question: Tell me about your current MPO project.
questions.answer:
A strong answer:
“My current project is a large enterprise application where one of the technically challenging areas is the map and track-history experience. We use React with Mapbox-based rendering and need to display vehicle/location history containing roughly 80K or more geographic points. The challenge is not simply plotting the points; it is keeping zoom in/out and map interactions responsive while avoiding unnecessary processing and rendering. We introduced a processing pipeline around viewport/bounds filtering, movement-based reduction, zoom-dependent sampling and distance-based reduction. We also measured raw, visible and rendered point counts and pipeline timings to identify bottlenecks. Alongside that, the application has Redux-based state management, API-driven modules and localization/translation requirements. The important engineering lesson was to treat rendering performance as a data-processing problem as well as a UI problem: reduce the amount of work before Mapbox receives the data.”

questions.question: What was the biggest technical challenge?
questions.answer: “The biggest challenge was rendering a very large track-history dataset while keeping zoom and pan interactions responsive. At certain zoom levels, the visible dataset could still be close to the complete raw dataset, so simply filtering by bounds was not enough. We therefore worked on adaptive reduction based on zoom, movement and geographic distance, and measured each stage instead of optimizing blindly.”

questions.question: What exactly did you optimize?
questions.answer: “I looked at the complete pipeline: raw data, bounds filtering, movement filtering, zoom sampling, distance reduction and GeoJSON construction. I tracked counts and timings for each stage. The goal was to reduce the number of points passed to the rendering layer while preserving the visual shape and useful track information.”

sections.title: L2. The 80K+ Mapbox Problem — Deep Questions

questions.question: Why is rendering 80K points difficult?
questions.answer: “The difficulty is the total amount of work, not just the number 80K. If every zoom/pan operation causes filtering, transformation, GeoJSON creation and rendering of tens of thousands of objects, the browser main thread can become busy and interaction becomes sluggish. Map rendering also has its own CPU/GPU and source/layer update costs.”

questions.question: Why didn't viewport/bounds filtering solve the problem?
questions.answer: “Because the viewport can still contain most or all of the dataset. For example, if the track covers an area currently visible on screen, bounds filtering may return almost the same number of points as the raw dataset. So bounds filtering is necessary but not sufficient; we need density-aware reduction or zoom-based sampling as well.”

questions.question: Explain your map processing pipeline.
questions.answer:
“The conceptual pipeline is: receive raw track history → apply time/duration rules → determine the current map bounds → filter points outside the viewport → apply movement/quality filtering → apply zoom-dependent sampling → reduce points by geographic distance where required → build the final GeoJSON/source data → render through Mapbox.”
Raw Track History
      ↓
Time / duration filter
      ↓
Viewport / bounds filter
      ↓
Movement filter
      ↓
Zoom-based sampling
      ↓
Distance reduction
      ↓
GeoJSON construction
      ↓
Mapbox source/layer
      ↓
Rendered track

questions.question: How did zoom affect rendering?
questions.answer: “At higher zoom levels, users need more geographic detail, so we can keep more points. At lower zoom levels, many nearby points visually overlap and displaying every point provides little additional value. Therefore the sampling threshold can become more aggressive as zoom decreases and less aggressive as zoom increases.”

questions.question: What does meters-per-pixel mean and why is it useful?
questions.answer: “Meters-per-pixel estimates the real-world geographic distance represented by one screen pixel at the current map zoom/location. It gives us a screen-space basis for deciding whether two geographic points are visually distinguishable. If two points are much closer than the useful pixel resolution, keeping both may not improve what the user sees.”

questions.question: Why not simply use one fixed distance threshold?
questions.answer: “A fixed geographic threshold behaves differently at different zoom levels. A distance that is visually tiny when zoomed out can become visibly significant when zoomed in. The threshold therefore needs to adapt to the current map resolution and potentially dataset density.”

questions.question: How did dataset size affect your strategy?
questions.answer: “The same algorithm does not necessarily work equally well for 2,000 and 85,000 points. We considered dataset size when tuning reduction so very large datasets receive stronger sampling at appropriate zoom levels, while smaller datasets can preserve more detail.”

questions.question: How did you verify that the optimization did not destroy the track?
questions.answer: “I compared raw versus visible versus rendered point counts and visually checked the track at different zoom levels. I also measured processing time. The goal was not simply to minimize the point count; it was to maintain the important shape, turns and movement information while reducing redundant points.”

questions.question: What metrics did you log?
questions.answer: “Useful metrics included total/raw points, visible points, final/rendered points, zoom level, meters-per-pixel or threshold information, bounds filtering time, reduction time, GeoJSON build time and total pipeline time. This helped identify whether the bottleneck was filtering, reduction, data construction or rendering.”

questions.question: Why can the UI freeze even when your filtering function is only tens of milliseconds?
questions.answer: “Because the measured function may be only one stage. The browser can also spend time in object allocation, garbage collection, React updates, GeoJSON/source updates, Mapbox processing and rendering. A full performance trace is therefore more useful than looking at one console timer in isolation.”

questions.question: Why did you avoid putting heavy processing inside a Redux reducer?
questions.answer: “Reducers should remain predictable state-transition functions. Heavy geographic processing inside a reducer can make every state update expensive and can affect other consumers of the same Redux state. We preferred keeping raw state management separate from expensive processing logic so the optimization remained localized and reusable.”

questions.question: Why not mutate the original track-history array?
questions.answer: “Mutating shared Redux data can break predictable state updates and make debugging difficult. I prefer treating the raw dataset as immutable and producing the derived visible/rendered dataset separately.”

questions.question: Source vs layer in Mapbox — explain simply.
questions.answer: “A source contains the underlying geographic data. A layer describes how that source is visualized. Keeping data and styling separate allows us to update or style the same source through layers.”

questions.question: What happens when you update a large GeoJSON source repeatedly?
questions.answer: “The map library needs to process the updated source, potentially rebuild internal structures and trigger rendering work. If we send a huge GeoJSON payload on every small interaction, the update itself can become a bottleneck. Reducing update frequency and payload size is therefore important.”

questions.question: How would you optimize map zoom/pan events?
questions.answer: “I would avoid running the complete expensive pipeline for every raw event. I would use the map's event lifecycle appropriately, coalesce rapid updates, compare whether the viewport/zoom actually changed enough to require recomputation, cache reusable calculations where valid, and keep the rendered dataset as small as possible.”

questions.question: Should you process on every zoom event or after zoom finishes?
questions.answer: “It depends on UX requirements. During continuous interaction, a lighter representation can keep the map responsive, followed by a higher-detail recalculation after the interaction settles. If continuous detail is required, processing should be incremental and bounded rather than performing the maximum workload on every event.”

questions.question: Why is virtualization not directly the same as map optimization?
questions.answer: “List virtualization works because only visible DOM rows need to exist. A map has a different rendering pipeline, so the equivalent strategy is spatial/data reduction: only send the amount of geographic data that provides useful visual information at the current resolution.”

questions.question: Would a Web Worker solve everything?
questions.answer: “No. A Worker can move CPU-heavy JavaScript off the main thread, which can improve UI responsiveness, but it does not automatically reduce the amount of data, serialization/copying overhead or Mapbox rendering work. The first optimization should still be reducing unnecessary work. In our project we also had practical constraints around using a Worker, so we focused on optimizing the synchronous pipeline.”

questions.question: How would you improve this further if the dataset became 1 million points?
questions.answer: “I would move toward server-side or tile-based spatial aggregation, request only data relevant to the viewport/time range, use vector tiles or another spatial representation where appropriate, progressively load detail and keep client-side processing bounded. At that scale, simply optimizing an 80K-point JavaScript loop is not enough.”

questions.question: How did translations affect the application?
questions.answer: “Localization is a cross-cutting concern. Labels, transaction statuses, validation messages and navigation should come from translation resources rather than being hard-coded inside components. The important engineering concern is keeping UI logic independent from the actual displayed language.”

questions.question: What can break when switching languages?
questions.answer: “Text length can change significantly, which can break fixed-width layouts, buttons, tables and dialogs. Dates, numbers, currency and pluralization can also differ. I avoid hard-coded widths based on English text and test longer translated strings.”

questions.question: How would you design localization for a large ERP?
questions.answer: “Centralize translation keys, separate domain terminology from UI components, provide fallback behavior, avoid concatenating translated fragments, handle pluralization/date/number formatting correctly and make components flexible enough for different text lengths.”

questions.question: Why should we avoid constructing sentences by concatenating translated strings?
questions.answer: “Word order varies by language. A sentence built from separate fragments in English may be grammatically incorrect in another language. Prefer complete translation keys with interpolation variables.”

sections.title: L5. Node.js Performance — Add These to Your Interview

questions.question: If the frontend is fast but the API is slow, how do you investigate?
questions.answer: “Start with browser Network timing: DNS/connect/TTFB/download. Then correlate the request with backend logs using a request ID. On Node, inspect controller/service/database timings, event-loop delay, external calls, serialization and payload size. For MongoDB, inspect query plans and indexes.”

questions.question: How can a Node.js API become slow even though all database queries are fast?
questions.answer: “The bottleneck can be CPU-heavy JavaScript, synchronous filesystem/crypto work, large JSON serialization, external APIs, event-loop blocking, excessive middleware or connection/resource contention.”

questions.question: How would you detect event-loop blocking?
questions.answer: “Use Node performance/diagnostic tooling and monitor event-loop delay. Correlate spikes with CPU profiles, synchronous operations or expensive loops. A key symptom is that unrelated requests become slow at the same time.”

questions.question: Why is async code not automatically non-blocking?
questions.answer: “An async function can still execute expensive synchronous JavaScript before its first await or between awaits. async/await makes asynchronous control flow easier to read; it does not move CPU-heavy JavaScript to another thread.”

questions.question: How would you process a large report in Node?
questions.answer: “Avoid loading everything into memory if possible. Stream database/file results, process incrementally, use backpressure and move CPU-heavy transformations to worker threads or a separate job service when appropriate.”

questions.question: How would you handle a long-running ERP transaction/report request?
questions.answer: “I would consider making it asynchronous: create a job, return a job ID, process it in a worker/queue and expose status/download when complete. Keeping a normal HTTP request open for several minutes is usually less resilient.”

sections.title: L6. Docker — From Implementation to Execution

questions.question: Explain Docker to an interviewer in simple terms.
questions.answer: “Docker packages an application and its runtime dependencies into a container image so it can run consistently across environments. The image is the packaged template; a container is a running instance of that image.”

questions.question: Image vs container?
questions.answer: “An image is an immutable packaged filesystem and metadata used as the basis for containers. A container is a running or stopped instance created from an image.”

questions.question: Dockerfile vs docker-compose.yml?
questions.answer: “A Dockerfile explains how to build an application image. Compose describes how multiple services should run together—such as frontend, API, database or supporting services—with networking, volumes and environment configuration.”

questions.question: Explain a basic Docker implementation flow.
questions.answer:
“First create the Dockerfile, install dependencies and build the application. Then build an image, run a container locally, expose the required port, inspect logs, test the application and iterate. For multi-service applications, define Compose services and their networking/configuration.”
# Dockerfile example
FROM node:22-alpine

WORKDIR /app

COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci

COPY . .
RUN npm run build

EXPOSE 3000
CMD ["npm", "start"]

questions.question: What does docker build do?
questions.answer: “It reads the Dockerfile and build context and creates an image, executing each Dockerfile instruction as build layers where applicable.”

questions.question: What does docker run do?
questions.answer:
“It creates a container from an image and starts it. Options can publish ports, set environment variables, mount volumes, assign networks and control runtime behavior.”
docker build -t mpo-web .
docker run -p 3000:3000 --name mpo-web mpo-web
docker ps
docker logs mpo-web
docker stop mpo-web

questions.question: Why use multi-stage Docker builds?
questions.answer: “They let us build the application in one stage with development/build dependencies and copy only the required runtime artifacts into a smaller final image. This reduces image size and attack surface.”

questions.question: Why is Docker image size important?
questions.answer: “Smaller images generally transfer faster, start faster and contain fewer unnecessary packages. It also reduces the potential attack surface.”

questions.question: What should not be copied into a Docker image?
questions.answer:
“Secrets, local dependency folders such as node_modules when they can be installed reproducibly inside the image, Git history and unnecessary build artifacts. Use .dockerignore and environment/secret management appropriately.”
.dockerignore
node_modules
.next
.git
.env*
npm-debug.log
coverage

questions.question: How do containers communicate in Docker Compose?
questions.answer: “Compose creates a network where services can reach each other by service name. For example, an API can connect to a MongoDB service using the Mongo service name as the hostname rather than localhost.”

questions.question: Why doesn't localhost inside a container mean my host machine?
questions.answer: “Inside a container, localhost refers to that container itself. To communicate with another Compose service, use its service name. Host access requires an appropriate host gateway/network configuration.”

sections.title: L7. Deployment — From Code Commit to Production

questions.question: Explain the complete deployment lifecycle.
questions.answer:
“Developer commits code → CI checks out the repository → installs dependencies → runs lint/type checks/tests → builds the application/image → tags the artifact → pushes it to a container registry → deployment environment pulls the image → container/service starts → health checks verify it → traffic is routed to the new version → logs/metrics/errors are monitored. If the release is unhealthy, rollback uses the previous known-good artifact.”
Developer
   ↓
Git repository
   ↓
CI: install → lint → test → build
   ↓
Docker image
   ↓
Container registry
   ↓
Server / orchestration platform
   ↓
Container starts
   ↓
Health check
   ↓
Traffic
   ↓
Monitoring / logs

questions.question: What is a container registry?
questions.answer: “A registry stores and distributes container images. CI pushes a versioned image there, and deployment infrastructure pulls the exact image required for the release.”

questions.question: Why should images be versioned?
questions.answer: “A versioned tag or immutable digest lets us identify exactly what is deployed and makes rollback deterministic. A floating tag such as latest can be convenient but is less reliable for reproducible deployment.”

questions.question: What happens when deployment fails after the container starts?
questions.answer: “First check container logs and health-check status, configuration/environment variables, network connectivity, dependency availability and resource limits. If the release is unhealthy and rollback is safer, restore the previous known-good version.”

questions.question: What is a health check?
questions.answer: “A health check verifies whether the service is alive/ready to receive traffic. A robust deployment distinguishes liveness from readiness where the platform supports both.”

questions.question: How should environment variables work in deployment?
questions.answer: “Non-secret configuration can be injected through environment variables/configuration. Secrets should come from secure secret management rather than being committed or baked into the image. The application should validate required configuration at startup.”

questions.question: What is zero-downtime deployment?
questions.answer: “The new version is started and verified before old capacity is removed, with traffic shifted safely. Strategies include rolling, blue-green and canary deployments depending on infrastructure.”

questions.question: Blue-green vs rolling vs canary?
questions.answer: “Blue-green maintains two environments and switches traffic between them. Rolling replaces instances gradually. Canary sends a small percentage of traffic to the new version before broader rollout.”

questions.question: How do you troubleshoot 'works locally but not in Docker'?
questions.answer: “Compare Node/runtime versions, environment variables, filesystem paths, network hostnames, exposed ports, build output, OS assumptions and dependency installation. Then inspect container logs and execute commands inside the container to verify the runtime environment.”

questions.question: How do you identify whether a performance problem is frontend, API or database?
questions.answer: “Trace one user action end-to-end. Browser Performance/Network shows client timing; request IDs correlate with API logs; backend timings identify service/database time; MongoDB explain identifies query problems. This avoids optimizing the wrong layer.”

questions.question: What is a performance budget?
questions.answer: “A defined limit for important metrics such as JavaScript bundle size, API latency, rendering time or map dataset size. It turns performance from a one-time optimization into an engineering constraint.”

questions.question: What is the difference between optimization and measurement?
questions.answer: “Optimization is changing the system; measurement tells us whether the change actually improved the user experience. A senior engineer should establish a baseline, change one meaningful factor, compare results and watch production behavior.”

questions.question: How would you explain your biggest performance lesson from the map project?
questions.answer: “The biggest lesson is that rendering performance starts before rendering. If the application sends unnecessary data to the rendering layer, no amount of component-level memoization can fully compensate. Reducing data volume, controlling update frequency and adapting detail to the user's zoom level are architectural performance decisions.”

sections.title: M. DOCKER — COMPLETE PRACTICAL & INTERVIEW MASTERCLASS

questions.question: What problem does Docker solve?
questions.answer: Docker packages an application together with its runtime environment and dependencies into a portable image. The goal is consistent execution across development, testing and deployment environments.

questions.question: What is containerization?
questions.answer: Containerization isolates an application's processes and filesystem view while sharing the host operating system kernel. It is lighter than running a complete virtual machine for many workloads.

questions.question: Docker vs virtual machine?
questions.answer: A VM virtualizes hardware and normally runs a complete guest operating system. A container shares the host kernel and isolates processes. Containers generally start faster and use fewer resources, while VMs provide stronger OS-level isolation.

questions.question: What is a Docker image?
questions.answer: An image is a read-only, layered package containing the filesystem and metadata needed to create containers.

questions.question: What is a container?
questions.answer: A running or stopped instance created from an image, with its own writable container layer and runtime configuration.

questions.question: What is Docker Engine?
questions.answer: The Docker runtime/platform that builds images and creates/runs containers, networks and volumes.

questions.question: What is Docker Hub?
questions.answer: A public/private container image registry service. Organizations can also use private registries such as cloud/container-registry products.

questions.question: What is a Docker registry?
questions.answer: A service that stores and distributes container images. CI can push versioned images and deployment infrastructure can pull them.

questions.question: What is a Docker tag?
questions.answer: A human-readable label associated with an image reference, commonly used for versions such as 1.4.2 or a release identifier.

questions.question: Tag vs digest?
questions.answer:
A tag is mutable by convention; a content digest identifies an exact image content. Production deployments benefit from immutable references/digests for reproducibility.
M2. Dockerfile — Line by Line

questions.question: Explain this Dockerfile.
questions.answer:
FROM node:22-alpine

WORKDIR /app

COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci

COPY . .
RUN npm run build

EXPOSE 3000

CMD ["npm", "start"]
FROM selects the base image. WORKDIR sets the working directory. COPY package files copies dependency manifests first so that dependency installation can be cached when application source changes. RUN npm ci installs dependencies reproducibly. COPY . . adds application source. RUN npm run build creates the production build. EXPOSE documents the intended container port. CMD defines the default process.

questions.question: Why copy package.json before the source code?
questions.answer: Docker builds in layers. If package manifests have not changed, the dependency-install layer can be reused even when source files change. This makes repeated builds faster.

questions.question: RUN vs CMD vs ENTRYPOINT?
questions.answer: RUN executes during image build. CMD defines the default command/arguments when a container starts and can be overridden. ENTRYPOINT defines the executable the container is intended to run and is harder to replace with normal command arguments. The combination depends on the desired image behavior.

questions.question: What is WORKDIR?
questions.answer: It sets the working directory for subsequent Dockerfile instructions and the default working directory for the container process.

questions.question: What does EXPOSE actually do?
questions.answer: It documents the port the image intends to use. It does not by itself publish the port to the host. Port publishing is done at runtime with options such as -p or through orchestration configuration.

questions.question: What is .dockerignore?
questions.answer:
It prevents unnecessary files from being sent in the Docker build context. This improves build speed and avoids accidentally copying local files, credentials or large directories.
.dockerignore
node_modules
.git
.next
coverage
.env
.env.*
npm-debug.log
Dockerfile*
docker-compose*.yml
M3. Node.js / Next.js Production Docker Patterns

questions.question: How would you Dockerize a Node.js API?
questions.answer: Use a small supported Node base image, copy dependency manifests, install production dependencies, copy the application, run any required build step, expose the API port and start the server with a production command. Prefer a non-root runtime user where practical.

questions.question: How would you Dockerize a Next.js application?
questions.answer:
For a production Next.js application, build the application in a builder stage and copy only the required production output and dependencies into a smaller runtime stage. The exact files depend on the Next.js output configuration and version.
# Example multi-stage pattern
FROM node:22-alpine AS builder
WORKDIR /app

COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci

COPY . .
RUN npm run build

FROM node:22-alpine AS runner
WORKDIR /app
ENV NODE_ENV=production

COPY --from=builder /app/package*.json ./
RUN npm ci --omit=dev

COPY --from=builder /app/.next ./.next
COPY --from=builder /app/public ./public

EXPOSE 3000
CMD ["npm", "start"]
In an actual Next.js project, use the framework's recommended production output strategy rather than blindly copying every build directory. If using standalone output, the runtime image can be made substantially smaller by copying the generated standalone artifacts and required static/public files.

questions.question: Why use multi-stage builds?
questions.answer: The builder can contain compilers, development dependencies and build tools. The final image contains only what is required to run the application. This reduces size and unnecessary packages.

questions.question: Why use npm ci instead of npm install in CI/Docker builds?
questions.answer: npm ci is designed for clean, reproducible installs from the lockfile and typically avoids modifying it. It is preferred when reproducibility matters.

questions.question: Should node_modules from your Mac be copied into a Linux image?
questions.answer: No. Native dependencies can be platform-specific. Install dependencies inside the image for the target Linux environment.

questions.question: Why can a Dockerized Node application work locally but fail in production?
questions.answer:
Possible causes include different Node versions, missing environment variables, incorrect filesystem assumptions, architecture-specific dependencies, incorrect ports, network hostnames, missing build artifacts or permissions.
M4. Docker Build Process

questions.question: Explain docker build.
questions.answer:
docker build -t mpo-web:1.0.0 .
Docker sends the build context to the builder, reads the Dockerfile and executes its instructions to produce an image. The -t option gives the resulting image a repository/name and tag.

questions.question: What is the build context?
questions.answer: The set of files made available to the Docker build. The final dot in docker build -t app . means the current directory is the context. .dockerignore reduces that context.

questions.question: What are Docker image layers?
questions.answer: Dockerfile instructions can create reusable layers. When earlier layers remain unchanged, the builder can reuse cached results, improving build performance.

questions.question: How do you reduce Docker build time?
questions.answer:
Use an effective .dockerignore, copy dependency manifests before source code, avoid unnecessary build steps, use build cache appropriately, use multi-stage builds and keep the build context small.
M5. Running Containers

questions.question: Explain these commands.
questions.answer:
docker images
docker ps
docker ps -a
docker run -d --name mpo-web -p 3000:3000 mpo-web:1.0.0
docker logs -f mpo-web
docker exec -it mpo-web sh
docker inspect mpo-web
docker stop mpo-web
docker rm mpo-web
docker images lists local images. docker ps shows running containers. docker ps -a includes stopped containers. docker run creates/starts a container. logs shows container output. exec opens a command inside a running container. inspect shows metadata/configuration. stop requests shutdown. rm removes the container.

questions.question: What does -p 3000:3000 mean?
questions.answer: Host port 3000 is mapped to container port 3000. A request to the host's port reaches the application's container port.

questions.question: What does -d mean?
questions.answer: Detached mode: the container runs in the background.

questions.question: How do you pass environment variables?
questions.answer:
docker run -e NODE_ENV=production   -e API_BASE_URL=https://api.example.com   -p 3000:3000 mpo-web:1.0.0
For larger deployments, configuration should normally be injected by the orchestration/platform rather than hard-coded into the command.

questions.question: How do you inspect a failing container?
questions.answer:
Start with docker ps -a and docker logs. Then inspect environment/configuration, ports, mounted files, network connectivity and the actual command. If it stays alive long enough, use docker exec to inspect the filesystem and processes.
M6. Docker Compose — Multi-Service Application

questions.question: Why use Docker Compose?
questions.answer:
Compose describes and runs multiple related services together. For local development, an ERP could have an API, frontend, MongoDB, Redis and supporting services.
services:
  api:
    build: ./api
    ports:
      - "4000:4000"
    environment:
      MONGO_URI: mongodb://mongo:27017/erp
    depends_on:
      - mongo

  mongo:
    image: mongo:8
    ports:
      - "27017:27017"
    volumes:
      - mongo_data:/data/db

volumes:
  mongo_data:

questions.question: Why is the API connecting to mongo rather than localhost?
questions.answer: Inside a Compose network, services can reach each other using service names. localhost inside the API container refers to the API container itself.

questions.question: What is a Docker volume?
questions.answer: A volume stores persistent data outside the container's writable layer. It is useful for databases where data must survive container replacement.

questions.question: Bind mount vs named volume?
questions.answer: A bind mount maps a host path into the container and is useful for development/source sharing. A named volume is managed by Docker and is commonly better suited for persistent application data.

questions.question: Should MongoDB data be stored only in a container filesystem?
questions.answer:
No for persistent environments. The container can be replaced, so database data should use durable storage/volumes or a managed database service.
M7. Docker Networking

questions.question: Explain Docker networking.
questions.answer: Containers can communicate through Docker networks. A Compose application normally creates a private network where services can reach one another by service name.

questions.question: What is port publishing vs container networking?
questions.answer: Port publishing exposes a container service through the host. Container networking allows services to communicate internally without necessarily exposing their ports publicly.

questions.question: Why should MongoDB not necessarily expose port 27017 publicly?
questions.answer: If only the API needs MongoDB, the database can remain on the internal network. Exposing it publicly increases attack surface and is usually unnecessary.

questions.question: How would you troubleshoot container connectivity?
questions.answer:
Verify both services are running, inspect their networks, confirm the hostname/service name and port, test DNS/connectivity from inside the container and check application configuration.
M8. Docker Volumes, Storage & Files

questions.question: What happens to container data when the container is removed?
questions.answer: Data in the container's writable layer is removed with the container. Persistent data should be placed in a volume or external storage.

questions.question: Why are volumes important for databases?
questions.answer: Database state must survive application/container replacement, restart or deployment.

questions.question: What about user-uploaded files?
questions.answer:
Do not assume the container filesystem is durable. Use object storage or persistent storage designed for the workload, and store only metadata in the database where appropriate.
M9. Docker Security

questions.question: Should containers run as root?
questions.answer: Prefer a non-root application user when possible. Running as root increases the impact of a container compromise.

questions.question: Should secrets be baked into Docker images?
questions.answer: No. Image layers can persist and be distributed. Inject secrets at runtime using secure secret-management mechanisms.

questions.question: Why pin base images?
questions.answer: A specific version/digest makes builds more reproducible and reduces unexpected changes. Base images should still be updated deliberately for security patches.

questions.question: How do you scan images?
questions.answer: Use an image/dependency vulnerability scanner in CI and establish policies for high-severity vulnerabilities.

questions.question: Why keep images minimal?
questions.answer: Fewer packages generally mean a smaller attack surface and fewer vulnerabilities to patch.

questions.question: What is the principle of least privilege in containers?
questions.answer:
Give the process only the filesystem, network, Linux capabilities and permissions it actually needs.
M10. Docker + CI/CD

questions.question: Explain a production Docker CI/CD pipeline.
questions.answer:
“A developer pushes code. CI checks out the commit, installs dependencies from the lockfile, runs lint/type checks/tests, builds the application and creates a Docker image. The image is tagged with the commit/release version and pushed to a registry. Deployment pulls that exact image, injects configuration/secrets, starts the new container and verifies health. If healthy, traffic moves to it; if unhealthy, the previous version remains available for rollback.”
git push
   ↓
CI
   ├── npm ci
   ├── lint
   ├── typecheck
   ├── test
   └── npm run build
          ↓
     docker build
          ↓
  image: mpo-web:<commit>
          ↓
   container registry
          ↓
      deployment
          ↓
   health / smoke test
          ↓
       traffic

questions.question: Why tag Docker images with Git commit SHA?
questions.answer: It provides a direct mapping between deployed artifact and source commit, which makes debugging and rollback easier.

questions.question: Why not deploy latest everywhere?
questions.answer: latest is mutable and does not clearly identify which artifact is running. Immutable release tags/digests make deployments reproducible.

questions.question: What is rollback?
questions.answer: Deploying the previous known-good application artifact/version when the new release is unhealthy or causes unacceptable regressions.

questions.question: What is a smoke test after deployment?
questions.answer:
A small set of high-value checks verifying that the service starts and critical functionality is reachable before considering the release healthy.
M11. Production Deployment Patterns

questions.question: Explain rolling deployment.
questions.answer: Replace instances gradually so capacity remains available while the new version is introduced. Health checks prevent unhealthy instances from receiving traffic.

questions.question: Explain blue-green deployment.
questions.answer: Run old and new environments simultaneously and switch traffic from blue to green after validation. Rollback can be fast by switching traffic back.

questions.question: Explain canary deployment.
questions.answer: Send a small percentage of traffic to the new version, observe metrics/errors, then gradually increase traffic if healthy.

questions.question: What metrics should you monitor after a Docker deployment?
questions.answer: Error rate, request latency, throughput, CPU, memory, restart count, event-loop delay for Node services, database latency, container health and key business metrics.

questions.question: What happens if the container repeatedly restarts?
questions.answer:
Inspect exit code and logs, verify startup command/configuration, environment variables, required dependencies, permissions and resource limits. A restart loop is a symptom; the application/container logs normally reveal the immediate cause.
M12. Docker Troubleshooting Interview Scenarios

questions.question: Docker says port is already allocated. What do you do?
questions.answer: Find the process/container using that host port with docker ps and appropriate host tooling, stop it or publish the new container on another host port.

questions.question: Container starts and immediately exits. Why?
questions.answer: The main process terminated, crashed or the command was incorrect. Check docker logs and inspect the container command/exit code.

questions.question: Application works on Mac but not in Linux container. What do you check?
questions.answer: Node version, native modules, case-sensitive filesystem paths, environment variables, architecture, permissions and OS-specific assumptions.

questions.question: Docker build is extremely slow. What do you inspect?
questions.answer: Build context size, missing .dockerignore, dependency layer invalidation, unnecessary COPY/RUN steps and cache usage.

questions.question: Image is 2GB. What would you do?
questions.answer: Inspect layers, remove unnecessary build tools from runtime using multi-stage builds, reduce dependencies and use an appropriate slim/alpine/distroless strategy after validating compatibility.

questions.question: Container can reach API but API cannot reach Mongo. What do you inspect?
questions.answer: Network membership, service hostname, Mongo port, connection string, Mongo readiness and authentication/configuration.

questions.question: New deployment has 500 errors but old version worked. What is your process?
questions.answer: Check logs/metrics, compare configuration and dependency versions, inspect database/API compatibility and reproduce the failing request. If impact is high, rollback first and investigate safely.

questions.question: Environment variable exists locally but is missing in production. Why?
questions.answer: Local .env files and shell environment are not automatically present in the production container. Deployment must explicitly inject the configuration.

questions.question: Why might a Docker health check fail while the process is running?
questions.answer:
The process may be alive but not ready, the health endpoint may be incorrect, the port may be wrong, dependencies may be unavailable or the check may run before startup completes.
M13. Docker Interview Command Sheet
# Build
docker build -t mpo-web:1.0.0 .

# Run
docker run -d --name mpo-web -p 3000:3000 mpo-web:1.0.0

# Inspect
docker ps
docker ps -a
docker images
docker inspect mpo-web

# Logs
docker logs mpo-web
docker logs -f mpo-web

# Shell
docker exec -it mpo-web sh

# Stop/remove
docker stop mpo-web
docker rm mpo-web

# Compose
docker compose up -d
docker compose ps
docker compose logs -f api
docker compose down

# Rebuild
docker compose build --no-cache
docker compose up -d
M14. Docker — 2-Minute Interview Answer
“I use Docker to make application deployment reproducible. We define the runtime in a Dockerfile, build an image and run that image as a container. For local multi-service development, Compose can define services such as the API, frontend and database, including networking and persistent volumes. For production, CI runs tests and builds a versioned image, pushes it to a private registry, and the deployment environment pulls that exact artifact. Configuration and secrets are injected at runtime rather than baked into the image. After deployment, health checks and monitoring verify the new version, and because the previous image remains available we can roll back if necessary. The main things I pay attention to are reproducibility, image size, security, persistent data, networking, observability and rollback.”
