Git repository
   ↓
CI: install → lint → test → build
   ↓
Docker image
   ↓
Container registry
   ↓
Server / orchestration platform
   ↓
Container starts
   ↓
Health check
   ↓
Traffic
   ↓
Monitoring / logs
questions.part: PART XIII — EXTENDED TOPICS & QUESTION BANK
questions.section: L7. Deployment — From Code Commit to Production

questions.question: What is a container registry?
questions.answer: “A registry stores and distributes container images. CI pushes a versioned image there, and deployment infrastructure pulls the exact image required for the release.”
questions.part: PART XIII — EXTENDED TOPICS & QUESTION BANK
questions.section: L7. Deployment — From Code Commit to Production

questions.question: Why should images be versioned?
questions.answer: “A versioned tag or immutable digest lets us identify exactly what is deployed and makes rollback deterministic. A floating tag such as latest can be convenient but is less reliable for reproducible deployment.”
questions.part: PART XIII — EXTENDED TOPICS & QUESTION BANK
questions.section: L7. Deployment — From Code Commit to Production

questions.question: What happens when deployment fails after the container starts?
questions.answer: “First check container logs and health-check status, configuration/environment variables, network connectivity, dependency availability and resource limits. If the release is unhealthy and rollback is safer, restore the previous known-good version.”
questions.part: PART XIII — EXTENDED TOPICS & QUESTION BANK
questions.section: L7. Deployment — From Code Commit to Production

questions.question: What is a health check?
questions.answer: “A health check verifies whether the service is alive/ready to receive traffic. A robust deployment distinguishes liveness from readiness where the platform supports both.”
questions.part: PART XIII — EXTENDED TOPICS & QUESTION BANK
questions.section: L7. Deployment — From Code Commit to Production

questions.question: How should environment variables work in deployment?
questions.answer: “Non-secret configuration can be injected through environment variables/configuration. Secrets should come from secure secret management rather than being committed or baked into the image. The application should validate required configuration at startup.”
questions.part: PART XIII — EXTENDED TOPICS & QUESTION BANK
questions.section: L7. Deployment — From Code Commit to Production

questions.question: What is zero-downtime deployment?
questions.answer: “The new version is started and verified before old capacity is removed, with traffic shifted safely. Strategies include rolling, blue-green and canary deployments depending on infrastructure.”
questions.part: PART XIII — EXTENDED TOPICS & QUESTION BANK
questions.section: L7. Deployment — From Code Commit to Production

questions.question: Blue-green vs rolling vs canary?
questions.answer: “Blue-green maintains two environments and switches traffic between them. Rolling replaces instances gradually. Canary sends a small percentage of traffic to the new version before broader rollout.”
questions.part: PART XIII — EXTENDED TOPICS & QUESTION BANK
questions.section: L7. Deployment — From Code Commit to Production

questions.question: How do you troubleshoot 'works locally but not in Docker'?
questions.answer: “Compare Node/runtime versions, environment variables, filesystem paths, network hostnames, exposed ports, build output, OS assumptions and dependency installation. Then inspect container logs and execute commands inside the container to verify the runtime environment.”
questions.part: PART XIII — EXTENDED TOPICS & QUESTION BANK
questions.section: L7. Deployment — From Code Commit to Production

questions.question: How do you identify whether a performance problem is frontend, API or database?
questions.answer: “Trace one user action end-to-end. Browser Performance/Network shows client timing; request IDs correlate with API logs; backend timings identify service/database time; MongoDB explain identifies query problems. This avoids optimizing the wrong layer.”
questions.part: PART XIII — EXTENDED TOPICS & QUESTION BANK

questions.question: What is a performance budget?
questions.answer: “A defined limit for important metrics such as JavaScript bundle size, API latency, rendering time or map dataset size. It turns performance from a one-time optimization into an engineering constraint.”
questions.part: PART XIII — EXTENDED TOPICS & QUESTION BANK

questions.question: What is the difference between optimization and measurement?
questions.answer: “Optimization is changing the system; measurement tells us whether the change actually improved the user experience. A senior engineer should establish a baseline, change one meaningful factor, compare results and watch production behavior.”
questions.part: PART XIII — EXTENDED TOPICS & QUESTION BANK

questions.question: How would you explain your biggest performance lesson from the map project?
questions.answer: “The biggest lesson is that rendering performance starts before rendering. If the application sends unnecessary data to the rendering layer, no amount of component-level memoization can fully compensate. Reducing data volume, controlling update frequency and adapting detail to the user's zoom level are architectural performance decisions.”
questions.part: PART XIII — EXTENDED TOPICS & QUESTION BANK

questions.question: What problem does Docker solve?
questions.answer: Docker packages an application together with its runtime environment and dependencies into a portable image. The goal is consistent execution across development, testing and deployment environments.
questions.part: PART XIII — EXTENDED TOPICS & QUESTION BANK
questions.section: M. DOCKER — COMPLETE PRACTICAL & INTERVIEW MASTERCLASS

questions.question: What is containerization?
questions.answer: Containerization isolates an application's processes and filesystem view while sharing the host operating system kernel. It is lighter than running a complete virtual machine for many workloads.
questions.part: PART XIII — EXTENDED TOPICS & QUESTION BANK
questions.section: M. DOCKER — COMPLETE PRACTICAL & INTERVIEW MASTERCLASS

questions.question: Docker vs virtual machine?
questions.answer: A VM virtualizes hardware and normally runs a complete guest operating system. A container shares the host kernel and isolates processes. Containers generally start faster and use fewer resources, while VMs provide stronger OS-level isolation.
questions.part: PART XIII — EXTENDED TOPICS & QUESTION BANK
questions.section: M. DOCKER — COMPLETE PRACTICAL & INTERVIEW MASTERCLASS

questions.question: What is a Docker image?
questions.answer: An image is a read-only, layered package containing the filesystem and metadata needed to create containers.
questions.part: PART XIII — EXTENDED TOPICS & QUESTION BANK
questions.section: M. DOCKER — COMPLETE PRACTICAL & INTERVIEW MASTERCLASS

questions.question: What is a container?
questions.answer: A running or stopped instance created from an image, with its own writable container layer and runtime configuration.
questions.part: PART XIII — EXTENDED TOPICS & QUESTION BANK
questions.section: M. DOCKER — COMPLETE PRACTICAL & INTERVIEW MASTERCLASS

questions.question: What is Docker Engine?
questions.answer: The Docker runtime/platform that builds images and creates/runs containers, networks and volumes.
questions.part: PART XIII — EXTENDED TOPICS & QUESTION BANK
questions.section: M. DOCKER — COMPLETE PRACTICAL & INTERVIEW MASTERCLASS

questions.question: What is Docker Hub?
questions.answer: A public/private container image registry service. Organizations can also use private registries such as cloud/container-registry products.
questions.part: PART XIII — EXTENDED TOPICS & QUESTION BANK
questions.section: M. DOCKER — COMPLETE PRACTICAL & INTERVIEW MASTERCLASS

questions.question: What is a Docker registry?
questions.answer: A service that stores and distributes container images. CI can push versioned images and deployment infrastructure can pull them.
questions.part: PART XIII — EXTENDED TOPICS & QUESTION BANK
questions.section: M. DOCKER — COMPLETE PRACTICAL & INTERVIEW MASTERCLASS

questions.question: What is a Docker tag?
questions.answer: A human-readable label associated with an image reference, commonly used for versions such as 1.4.2 or a release identifier.
questions.part: PART XIII — EXTENDED TOPICS & QUESTION BANK
questions.section: M. DOCKER — COMPLETE PRACTICAL & INTERVIEW MASTERCLASS

questions.question: Tag vs digest?
questions.answer:
A tag is mutable by convention; a content digest identifies an exact image content. Production deployments benefit from immutable references/digests for reproducibility.
M2. Dockerfile — Line by Line
questions.part: PART XIII — EXTENDED TOPICS & QUESTION BANK
questions.section: M. DOCKER — COMPLETE PRACTICAL & INTERVIEW MASTERCLASS

questions.question: Explain this Dockerfile.
questions.answer:
FROM node:22-alpine

WORKDIR /app

COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci

COPY . .
RUN npm run build

EXPOSE 3000

CMD ["npm", "start"]
FROM selects the base image. WORKDIR sets the working directory. COPY package files copies dependency manifests first so that dependency installation can be cached when application source changes. RUN npm ci installs dependencies reproducibly. COPY . . adds application source. RUN npm run build creates the production build. EXPOSE documents the intended container port. CMD defines the default process.
questions.part: PART XIII — EXTENDED TOPICS & QUESTION BANK
questions.section: M. DOCKER — COMPLETE PRACTICAL & INTERVIEW MASTERCLASS

questions.question: Why copy package.json before the source code?
questions.answer: Docker builds in layers. If package manifests have not changed, the dependency-install layer can be reused even when source files change. This makes repeated builds faster.
questions.part: PART XIII — EXTENDED TOPICS & QUESTION BANK
questions.section: M. DOCKER — COMPLETE PRACTICAL & INTERVIEW MASTERCLASS

questions.question: RUN vs CMD vs ENTRYPOINT?
questions.answer: RUN executes during image build. CMD defines the default command/arguments when a container starts and can be overridden. ENTRYPOINT defines the executable the container is intended to run and is harder to replace with normal command arguments. The combination depends on the desired image behavior.
questions.part: PART XIII — EXTENDED TOPICS & QUESTION BANK
questions.section: M. DOCKER — COMPLETE PRACTICAL & INTERVIEW MASTERCLASS

questions.question: What is WORKDIR?
questions.answer: It sets the working directory for subsequent Dockerfile instructions and the default working directory for the container process.
questions.part: PART XIII — EXTENDED TOPICS & QUESTION BANK
questions.section: M. DOCKER — COMPLETE PRACTICAL & INTERVIEW MASTERCLASS

questions.question: What does EXPOSE actually do?
questions.answer: It documents the port the image intends to use. It does not by itself publish the port to the host. Port publishing is done at runtime with options such as -p or through orchestration configuration.
questions.part: PART XIII — EXTENDED TOPICS & QUESTION BANK
questions.section: M. DOCKER — COMPLETE PRACTICAL & INTERVIEW MASTERCLASS

questions.question: What is .dockerignore?
questions.answer:
It prevents unnecessary files from being sent in the Docker build context. This improves build speed and avoids accidentally copying local files, credentials or large directories.
.dockerignore
node_modules
.git
.next
coverage
.env
.env.*
npm-debug.log
Dockerfile*
docker-compose*.yml
M3. Node.js / Next.js Production Docker Patterns
questions.part: PART XIII — EXTENDED TOPICS & QUESTION BANK
questions.section: M. DOCKER — COMPLETE PRACTICAL & INTERVIEW MASTERCLASS

questions.question: How would you Dockerize a Node.js API?
questions.answer: Use a small supported Node base image, copy dependency manifests, install production dependencies, copy the application, run any required build step, expose the API port and start the server with a production command. Prefer a non-root runtime user where practical.
questions.part: PART XIII — EXTENDED TOPICS & QUESTION BANK
questions.section: M. DOCKER — COMPLETE PRACTICAL & INTERVIEW MASTERCLASS

questions.question: How would you Dockerize a Next.js application?
questions.answer:
For a production Next.js application, build the application in a builder stage and copy only the required production output and dependencies into a smaller runtime stage. The exact files depend on the Next.js output configuration and version.
# Example multi-stage pattern
FROM node:22-alpine AS builder
WORKDIR /app

COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci

COPY . .
RUN npm run build

FROM node:22-alpine AS runner
WORKDIR /app
ENV NODE_ENV=production

COPY --from=builder /app/package*.json ./
RUN npm ci --omit=dev

COPY --from=builder /app/.next ./.next
COPY --from=builder /app/public ./public

EXPOSE 3000
CMD ["npm", "start"]
In an actual Next.js project, use the framework's recommended production output strategy rather than blindly copying every build directory. If using standalone output, the runtime image can be made substantially smaller by copying the generated standalone artifacts and required static/public files.
questions.part: PART XIII — EXTENDED TOPICS & QUESTION BANK
questions.section: M. DOCKER — COMPLETE PRACTICAL & INTERVIEW MASTERCLASS

questions.question: Why use multi-stage builds?
questions.answer: The builder can contain compilers, development dependencies and build tools. The final image contains only what is required to run the application. This reduces size and unnecessary packages.
questions.part: PART XIII — EXTENDED TOPICS & QUESTION BANK
questions.section: M. DOCKER — COMPLETE PRACTICAL & INTERVIEW MASTERCLASS

questions.question: Why use npm ci instead of npm install in CI/Docker builds?
questions.answer: npm ci is designed for clean, reproducible installs from the lockfile and typically avoids modifying it. It is preferred when reproducibility matters.
questions.part: PART XIII — EXTENDED TOPICS & QUESTION BANK
questions.section: M. DOCKER — COMPLETE PRACTICAL & INTERVIEW MASTERCLASS

questions.question: Should node_modules from your Mac be copied into a Linux image?
questions.answer: No. Native dependencies can be platform-specific. Install dependencies inside the image for the target Linux environment.
questions.part: PART XIII — EXTENDED TOPICS & QUESTION BANK
questions.section: M. DOCKER — COMPLETE PRACTICAL & INTERVIEW MASTERCLASS

questions.question: Why can a Dockerized Node application work locally but fail in production?
questions.answer:
Possible causes include different Node versions, missing environment variables, incorrect filesystem assumptions, architecture-specific dependencies, incorrect ports, network hostnames, missing build artifacts or permissions.
M4. Docker Build Process
questions.part: PART XIII — EXTENDED TOPICS & QUESTION BANK
questions.section: M. DOCKER — COMPLETE PRACTICAL & INTERVIEW MASTERCLASS

questions.question: Explain docker build.
questions.answer:
docker build -t mpo-web:1.0.0 .
Docker sends the build context to the builder, reads the Dockerfile and executes its instructions to produce an image. The -t option gives the resulting image a repository/name and tag.
questions.part: PART XIII — EXTENDED TOPICS & QUESTION BANK
questions.section: M. DOCKER — COMPLETE PRACTICAL & INTERVIEW MASTERCLASS

questions.question: What is the build context?
questions.answer: The set of files made available to the Docker build. The final dot in docker build -t app . means the current directory is the context. .dockerignore reduces that context.
questions.part: PART XIII — EXTENDED TOPICS & QUESTION BANK
questions.section: M. DOCKER — COMPLETE PRACTICAL & INTERVIEW MASTERCLASS

questions.question: What are Docker image layers?
questions.answer: Dockerfile instructions can create reusable layers. When earlier layers remain unchanged, the builder can reuse cached results, improving build performance.
questions.part: PART XIII — EXTENDED TOPICS & QUESTION BANK
questions.section: M. DOCKER — COMPLETE PRACTICAL & INTERVIEW MASTERCLASS

questions.question: How do you reduce Docker build time?
questions.answer:
Use an effective .dockerignore, copy dependency manifests before source code, avoid unnecessary build steps, use build cache appropriately, use multi-stage builds and keep the build context small.
M5. Running Containers
questions.part: PART XIII — EXTENDED TOPICS & QUESTION BANK
questions.section: M. DOCKER — COMPLETE PRACTICAL & INTERVIEW MASTERCLASS

questions.question: Explain these commands.
questions.answer:
docker images
docker ps
docker ps -a
docker run -d --name mpo-web -p 3000:3000 mpo-web:1.0.0
docker logs -f mpo-web
docker exec -it mpo-web sh
docker inspect mpo-web
docker stop mpo-web
docker rm mpo-web
docker images lists local images. docker ps shows running containers. docker ps -a includes stopped containers. docker run creates/starts a container. logs shows container output. exec opens a command inside a running container. inspect shows metadata/configuration. stop requests shutdown. rm removes the container.
questions.part: PART XIII — EXTENDED TOPICS & QUESTION BANK
questions.section: M. DOCKER — COMPLETE PRACTICAL & INTERVIEW MASTERCLASS

questions.question: What does -p 3000:3000 mean?
questions.answer: Host port 3000 is mapped to container port 3000. A request to the host's port reaches the application's container port.
questions.part: PART XIII — EXTENDED TOPICS & QUESTION BANK
questions.section: M. DOCKER — COMPLETE PRACTICAL & INTERVIEW MASTERCLASS

questions.question: What does -d mean?
questions.answer: Detached mode: the container runs in the background.
questions.part: PART XIII — EXTENDED TOPICS & QUESTION BANK
questions.section: M. DOCKER — COMPLETE PRACTICAL & INTERVIEW MASTERCLASS

questions.question: How do you pass environment variables?
questions.answer:
docker run -e NODE_ENV=production   -e API_BASE_URL=https://api.example.com   -p 3000:3000 mpo-web:1.0.0
For larger deployments, configuration should normally be injected by the orchestration/platform rather than hard-coded into the command.
questions.part: PART XIII — EXTENDED TOPICS & QUESTION BANK
questions.section: M. DOCKER — COMPLETE PRACTICAL & INTERVIEW MASTERCLASS

questions.question: How do you inspect a failing container?
questions.answer:
Start with docker ps -a and docker logs. Then inspect environment/configuration, ports, mounted files, network connectivity and the actual command. If it stays alive long enough, use docker exec to inspect the filesystem and processes.
M6. Docker Compose — Multi-Service Application
questions.part: PART XIII — EXTENDED TOPICS & QUESTION BANK
questions.section: M. DOCKER — COMPLETE PRACTICAL & INTERVIEW MASTERCLASS

questions.question: Why use Docker Compose?
questions.answer:
Compose describes and runs multiple related services together. For local development, an ERP could have an API, frontend, MongoDB, Redis and supporting services.
services:
  api:
    build: ./api
    ports:
      - "4000:4000"
    environment:
      MONGO_URI: mongodb://mongo:27017/erp
    depends_on:
      - mongo

  mongo:
    image: mongo:8
    ports:
      - "27017:27017"
    volumes:
      - mongo_data:/data/db

volumes:
  mongo_data:
questions.part: PART XIII — EXTENDED TOPICS & QUESTION BANK
questions.section: M. DOCKER — COMPLETE PRACTICAL & INTERVIEW MASTERCLASS

questions.question: Why is the API connecting to mongo rather than localhost?
questions.answer: Inside a Compose network, services can reach each other using service names. localhost inside the API container refers to the API container itself.
questions.part: PART XIII — EXTENDED TOPICS & QUESTION BANK
questions.section: M. DOCKER — COMPLETE PRACTICAL & INTERVIEW MASTERCLASS

questions.question: What is a Docker volume?
questions.answer: A volume stores persistent data outside the container's writable layer. It is useful for databases where data must survive container replacement.
questions.part: PART XIII — EXTENDED TOPICS & QUESTION BANK
questions.section: M. DOCKER — COMPLETE PRACTICAL & INTERVIEW MASTERCLASS

questions.question: Bind mount vs named volume?
questions.answer: A bind mount maps a host path into the container and is useful for development/source sharing. A named volume is managed by Docker and is commonly better suited for persistent application data.
questions.part: PART XIII — EXTENDED TOPICS & QUESTION BANK
questions.section: M. DOCKER — COMPLETE PRACTICAL & INTERVIEW MASTERCLASS

questions.question: Should MongoDB data be stored only in a container filesystem?
questions.answer:
No for persistent environments. The container can be replaced, so database data should use durable storage/volumes or a managed database service.
M7. Docker Networking
questions.part: PART XIII — EXTENDED TOPICS & QUESTION BANK
questions.section: M. DOCKER — COMPLETE PRACTICAL & INTERVIEW MASTERCLASS

questions.question: Explain Docker networking.
questions.answer: Containers can communicate through Docker networks. A Compose application normally creates a private network where services can reach one another by service name.
questions.part: PART XIII — EXTENDED TOPICS & QUESTION BANK
questions.section: M. DOCKER — COMPLETE PRACTICAL & INTERVIEW MASTERCLASS

questions.question: What is port publishing vs container networking?
questions.answer: Port publishing exposes a container service through the host. Container networking allows services to communicate internally without necessarily exposing their ports publicly.
questions.part: PART XIII — EXTENDED TOPICS & QUESTION BANK
questions.section: M. DOCKER — COMPLETE PRACTICAL & INTERVIEW MASTERCLASS

questions.question: Why should MongoDB not necessarily expose port 27017 publicly?
questions.answer: If only the API needs MongoDB, the database can remain on the internal network. Exposing it publicly increases attack surface and is usually unnecessary.
questions.part: PART XIII — EXTENDED TOPICS & QUESTION BANK
questions.section: M. DOCKER — COMPLETE PRACTICAL & INTERVIEW MASTERCLASS

questions.question: How would you troubleshoot container connectivity?
questions.answer:
Verify both services are running, inspect their networks, confirm the hostname/service name and port, test DNS/connectivity from inside the container and check application configuration.
M8. Docker Volumes, Storage & Files
questions.part: PART XIII — EXTENDED TOPICS & QUESTION BANK
questions.section: M. DOCKER — COMPLETE PRACTICAL & INTERVIEW MASTERCLASS

questions.question: What happens to container data when the container is removed?
questions.answer: Data in the container's writable layer is removed with the container. Persistent data should be placed in a volume or external storage.
questions.part: PART XIII — EXTENDED TOPICS & QUESTION BANK
questions.section: M. DOCKER — COMPLETE PRACTICAL & INTERVIEW MASTERCLASS

questions.question: Why are volumes important for databases?
questions.answer: Database state must survive application/container replacement, restart or deployment.
questions.part: PART XIII — EXTENDED TOPICS & QUESTION BANK
questions.section: M. DOCKER — COMPLETE PRACTICAL & INTERVIEW MASTERCLASS

questions.question: What about user-uploaded files?
questions.answer:
Do not assume the container filesystem is durable. Use object storage or persistent storage designed for the workload, and store only metadata in the database where appropriate.
M9. Docker Security
questions.part: PART XIII — EXTENDED TOPICS & QUESTION BANK
questions.section: M. DOCKER — COMPLETE PRACTICAL & INTERVIEW MASTERCLASS

questions.question: Should containers run as root?
questions.answer: Prefer a non-root application user when possible. Running as root increases the impact of a container compromise.
questions.part: PART XIII — EXTENDED TOPICS & QUESTION BANK
questions.section: M. DOCKER — COMPLETE PRACTICAL & INTERVIEW MASTERCLASS

questions.question: Should secrets be baked into Docker images?
questions.answer: No. Image layers can persist and be distributed. Inject secrets at runtime using secure secret-management mechanisms.
questions.part: PART XIII — EXTENDED TOPICS & QUESTION BANK
questions.section: M. DOCKER — COMPLETE PRACTICAL & INTERVIEW MASTERCLASS

questions.question: Why pin base images?
questions.answer: A specific version/digest makes builds more reproducible and reduces unexpected changes. Base images should still be updated deliberately for security patches.
questions.part: PART XIII — EXTENDED TOPICS & QUESTION BANK
questions.section: M. DOCKER — COMPLETE PRACTICAL & INTERVIEW MASTERCLASS

questions.question: How do you scan images?
questions.answer: Use an image/dependency vulnerability scanner in CI and establish policies for high-severity vulnerabilities.
questions.part: PART XIII — EXTENDED TOPICS & QUESTION BANK
questions.section: M. DOCKER — COMPLETE PRACTICAL & INTERVIEW MASTERCLASS

questions.question: Why keep images minimal?
questions.answer: Fewer packages generally mean a smaller attack surface and fewer vulnerabilities to patch.
questions.part: PART XIII — EXTENDED TOPICS & QUESTION BANK
questions.section: M. DOCKER — COMPLETE PRACTICAL & INTERVIEW MASTERCLASS

questions.question: What is the principle of least privilege in containers?
questions.answer:
Give the process only the filesystem, network, Linux capabilities and permissions it actually needs.
M10. Docker + CI/CD
questions.part: PART XIII — EXTENDED TOPICS & QUESTION BANK
questions.section: M. DOCKER — COMPLETE PRACTICAL & INTERVIEW MASTERCLASS

questions.question: Explain a production Docker CI/CD pipeline.
questions.answer:
“A developer pushes code. CI checks out the commit, installs dependencies from the lockfile, runs lint/type checks/tests, builds the application and creates a Docker image. The image is tagged with the commit/release version and pushed to a registry. Deployment pulls that exact image, injects configuration/secrets, starts the new container and verifies health. If healthy, traffic moves to it; if unhealthy, the previous version remains available for rollback.”
git push
   ↓
CI
   ├── npm ci
   ├── lint
   ├── typecheck
   ├── test
   └── npm run build
          ↓
     docker build
          ↓
  image: mpo-web:<commit>
          ↓
   container registry
          ↓
      deployment
          ↓
   health / smoke test
          ↓
       traffic
questions.part: PART XIII — EXTENDED TOPICS & QUESTION BANK
questions.section: M. DOCKER — COMPLETE PRACTICAL & INTERVIEW MASTERCLASS

questions.question: Why tag Docker images with Git commit SHA?
questions.answer: It provides a direct mapping between deployed artifact and source commit, which makes debugging and rollback easier.
questions.part: PART XIII — EXTENDED TOPICS & QUESTION BANK
questions.section: M. DOCKER — COMPLETE PRACTICAL & INTERVIEW MASTERCLASS

questions.question: Why not deploy latest everywhere?
questions.answer: latest is mutable and does not clearly identify which artifact is running. Immutable release tags/digests make deployments reproducible.
questions.part: PART XIII — EXTENDED TOPICS & QUESTION BANK
questions.section: M. DOCKER — COMPLETE PRACTICAL & INTERVIEW MASTERCLASS

questions.question: What is rollback?
questions.answer: Deploying the previous known-good application artifact/version when the new release is unhealthy or causes unacceptable regressions.
questions.part: PART XIII — EXTENDED TOPICS & QUESTION BANK
questions.section: M. DOCKER — COMPLETE PRACTICAL & INTERVIEW MASTERCLASS

questions.question: What is a smoke test after deployment?
questions.answer:
A small set of high-value checks verifying that the service starts and critical functionality is reachable before considering the release healthy.
M11. Production Deployment Patterns
questions.part: PART XIII — EXTENDED TOPICS & QUESTION BANK
questions.section: M. DOCKER — COMPLETE PRACTICAL & INTERVIEW MASTERCLASS

questions.question: Explain rolling deployment.
questions.answer: Replace instances gradually so capacity remains available while the new version is introduced. Health checks prevent unhealthy instances from receiving traffic.
questions.part: PART XIII — EXTENDED TOPICS & QUESTION BANK
questions.section: M. DOCKER — COMPLETE PRACTICAL & INTERVIEW MASTERCLASS

questions.question: Explain blue-green deployment.
questions.answer: Run old and new environments simultaneously and switch traffic from blue to green after validation. Rollback can be fast by switching traffic back.
questions.part: PART XIII — EXTENDED TOPICS & QUESTION BANK
questions.section: M. DOCKER — COMPLETE PRACTICAL & INTERVIEW MASTERCLASS

questions.question: Explain canary deployment.
questions.answer: Send a small percentage of traffic to the new version, observe metrics/errors, then gradually increase traffic if healthy.
questions.part: PART XIII — EXTENDED TOPICS & QUESTION BANK
questions.section: M. DOCKER — COMPLETE PRACTICAL & INTERVIEW MASTERCLASS

questions.question: What metrics should you monitor after a Docker deployment?
questions.answer: Error rate, request latency, throughput, CPU, memory, restart count, event-loop delay for Node services, database latency, container health and key business metrics.
questions.part: PART XIII — EXTENDED TOPICS & QUESTION BANK
questions.section: M. DOCKER — COMPLETE PRACTICAL & INTERVIEW MASTERCLASS

questions.question: What happens if the container repeatedly restarts?
questions.answer:
Inspect exit code and logs, verify startup command/configuration, environment variables, required dependencies, permissions and resource limits. A restart loop is a symptom; the application/container logs normally reveal the immediate cause.
M12. Docker Troubleshooting Interview Scenarios
questions.part: PART XIII — EXTENDED TOPICS & QUESTION BANK
questions.section: M. DOCKER — COMPLETE PRACTICAL & INTERVIEW MASTERCLASS

questions.question: Docker says port is already allocated. What do you do?
questions.answer: Find the process/container using that host port with docker ps and appropriate host tooling, stop it or publish the new container on another host port.
questions.part: PART XIII — EXTENDED TOPICS & QUESTION BANK
questions.section: M. DOCKER — COMPLETE PRACTICAL & INTERVIEW MASTERCLASS

questions.question: Container starts and immediately exits. Why?
questions.answer: The main process terminated, crashed or the command was incorrect. Check docker logs and inspect the container command/exit code.
questions.part: PART XIII — EXTENDED TOPICS & QUESTION BANK
questions.section: M. DOCKER — COMPLETE PRACTICAL & INTERVIEW MASTERCLASS

questions.question: Application works on Mac but not in Linux container. What do you check?
questions.answer: Node version, native modules, case-sensitive filesystem paths, environment variables, architecture, permissions and OS-specific assumptions.
questions.part: PART XIII — EXTENDED TOPICS & QUESTION BANK
questions.section: M. DOCKER — COMPLETE PRACTICAL & INTERVIEW MASTERCLASS

questions.question: Docker build is extremely slow. What do you inspect?
questions.answer: Build context size, missing .dockerignore, dependency layer invalidation, unnecessary COPY/RUN steps and cache usage.
questions.part: PART XIII — EXTENDED TOPICS & QUESTION BANK
questions.section: M. DOCKER — COMPLETE PRACTICAL & INTERVIEW MASTERCLASS

questions.question: Image is 2GB. What would you do?
questions.answer: Inspect layers, remove unnecessary build tools from runtime using multi-stage builds, reduce dependencies and use an appropriate slim/alpine/distroless strategy after validating compatibility.
questions.part: PART XIII — EXTENDED TOPICS & QUESTION BANK
questions.section: M. DOCKER — COMPLETE PRACTICAL & INTERVIEW MASTERCLASS

questions.question: Container can reach API but API cannot reach Mongo. What do you inspect?
questions.answer: Network membership, service hostname, Mongo port, connection string, Mongo readiness and authentication/configuration.
questions.part: PART XIII — EXTENDED TOPICS & QUESTION BANK
questions.section: M. DOCKER — COMPLETE PRACTICAL & INTERVIEW MASTERCLASS

questions.question: New deployment has 500 errors but old version worked. What is your process?
questions.answer: Check logs/metrics, compare configuration and dependency versions, inspect database/API compatibility and reproduce the failing request. If impact is high, rollback first and investigate safely.
questions.part: PART XIII — EXTENDED TOPICS & QUESTION BANK
questions.section: M. DOCKER — COMPLETE PRACTICAL & INTERVIEW MASTERCLASS

questions.question: Environment variable exists locally but is missing in production. Why?
questions.answer: Local .env files and shell environment are not automatically present in the production container. Deployment must explicitly inject the configuration.
questions.part: PART XIII — EXTENDED TOPICS & QUESTION BANK
questions.section: M. DOCKER — COMPLETE PRACTICAL & INTERVIEW MASTERCLASS

questions.question: Why might a Docker health check fail while the process is running?
questions.answer:
The process may be alive but not ready, the health endpoint may be incorrect, the port may be wrong, dependencies may be unavailable or the check may run before startup completes.

docker build -t mpo-web:1.0.0 .

docker run -d --name mpo-web -p 3000:3000 mpo-web:1.0.0

# Inspect
docker ps
docker ps -a
docker images
docker inspect mpo-web

# Logs
docker logs mpo-web
docker logs -f mpo-web

docker exec -it mpo-web sh

# Stop/remove
docker stop mpo-web
docker rm mpo-web

# Compose
docker compose up -d
docker compose ps
docker compose logs -f api
docker compose down

# Rebuild
docker compose build --no-cache
docker compose up -d
M14. Docker — 2-Minute Interview Answer
“I use Docker to make application deployment reproducible. We define the runtime in a Dockerfile, build an image and run that image as a container. For local multi-service development, Compose can define services such as the API, frontend and database, including networking and persistent volumes. For production, CI runs tests and builds a versioned image, pushes it to a private registry, and the deployment environment pulls that exact artifact. Configuration and secrets are injected at runtime rather than baked into the image. After deployment, health checks and monitoring verify the new version, and because the previous image remains available we can roll back if necessary. The main things I pay attention to are reproducibility, image size, security, persistent data, networking, observability and rollback.”

questions.question: Arrow functions vs regular functions?
questions.answer: Arrow functions don't have their own this, arguments, super, or new.target — they lexically inherit this from the enclosing scope, so they can't be used as constructors and are a poor fit for object methods that rely on this. Regular functions get their own this (determined by how they're called), receive an arguments object, and can be used with new. Arrow functions also can't be generators.

questions.question: What is a higher-order function?
questions.answer: A function that takes one or more functions as arguments, returns a function, or both. They enable composition and abstraction over behavior — map, filter, reduce, and event-handler factories are all higher-order functions.

questions.question: What is currying?
questions.answer: Currying transforms a function that takes multiple arguments into a sequence of functions that each take a single argument, returning a new function until all arguments are supplied. It enables partial application and reusable, specialized functions.

questions.question: What is an IIFE (Immediately Invoked Function Expression)?
questions.answer: A function expression that runs as soon as it's defined, creating an isolated scope. Before ES modules and block-scoped let/const, IIFEs were the standard way to avoid polluting the global scope and to encapsulate private state (the module pattern).

questions.question: Default parameters vs rest parameters vs the arguments object?
questions.answer: Default parameters supply a fallback value when an argument is undefined. Rest parameters (...args) collect any remaining arguments into a real array. The legacy arguments object is an array-like (not a real array — no map/filter) available only in regular functions, not arrow functions, and reflects exactly what was passed in, not the defaults applied.

questions.question: What is a pure function?
questions.answer: A pure function always returns the same output for the same input and produces no observable side effects — no mutating arguments, no I/O, no reliance on external mutable state. Pure functions are easier to test, memoize, and reason about, which is central to React's rendering model and Redux reducers.

questions.question: What is a generator function?
questions.answer: A generator function (function*) can pause and resume execution using yield, returning an iterator. Each call to .next() runs until the next yield, making generators useful for lazy sequences, custom iterables, and — historically — flow control before async/await.
